subject: mathematics
question_text: In triangle ABC, O is the circumcentre and H is the orthocentre. Show that HA + HB + HC = 2HO.

mark_split.label: Write HA, HB, HC as differences from O

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.64, chapter 6 ADDITION OF VECTORS, Short Answer question 5(ii). Only the question was taken — the solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work, see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. METHOD CHOICE RECORDED: the book prints this as part (ii) of the same question as OA + OB + OC = OH, so a student answering only part (ii) in the examination may not have written part (i). The card is therefore authored to STAND ALONE — step three both states OA + OB + OC = OH and gives a one-bracket proof of it (the point P with OP = OA + OB + OC satisfies AP = 2 OD and BP = 2 OE, both perpendicular to the opposite sides, so P is the orthocentre). The result was checked a second way by substituting it back: HA + HB + HC = OH − 3 OH = −2 OH, and −OH is HO. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 split rewards rewriting each vector from the common point O, the addition, the quoted-and-justified first result, and the final sign change from −2 OH to 2 HO. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Addition of Vectors has no Section C slot on the paper, so the unit is SAQ and VSAQ only. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say which point you measure everything from, and which earlier result you use.

steps.label: Write HA, HB, HC from O
steps.margin_note: First mark. Everything in the question is measured from H, but the useful result is measured from O. Rewrite all three vectors from O first — after that the proof is arithmetic.
steps.memory_tip: Rewrite every vector from the point that has the useful result. Here that point is O: HX = OX − OH.
lines: Take O, the circumcentre, as the reference
point. For any point X,  HX = OX − OH.

recall.must_convey: That each of HA, HB, HC is rewritten from the circumcentre O as OA − OH, OB − OH and OC − OH.
accept: write HA as OA minus OH and do the same for HB and HC
measure everything from O instead of from H
any vector HX is OX minus OH
anni vectors ni O nunchi rasi, HA equals OA minus OH
change the reference point to the circumcentre

steps.why: A vector between two points is the difference of their position vectors from any one chosen point. Choosing O is what lets the known circumcentre result be used later.
common_mistakes: Writing HA = OH − OA, which reverses every term in the answer.
Keeping H as the reference point, which leaves nothing to substitute.

steps.label: Add the three vectors
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Add the three lines as they stand. The OH term appears three times, so it collects as 3 OH — losing that 3 is the commonest slip on this question.
steps.memory_tip: Three vectors, three copies of OH. The sum carries −3 OH, not −OH.

recall.must_convey: That adding the three gives (OA + OB + OC) − 3 OH, with the OH term counted three times.
accept: add the three and you get OA plus OB plus OC minus three OH
the OH term appears three times so it becomes three OH
collect the position vectors together and the OH terms together
moodu saarlu OH vasthundi kabatti three OH
the sum is the three position vectors minus three OH

steps.why: Grouping the three position vectors on one side and the three copies of OH on the other is what makes the known result usable — the bracket that appears is exactly the one that has a value.
common_mistakes: Adding the magnitudes of the vectors instead of the vectors.

steps.label: Use OA + OB + OC = OH
steps.margin_note: Third mark. This is the standard circumcentre-to-orthocentre result. Quote it, and give the one-bracket reason so the answer stands on its own even if part (i) was not attempted.
steps.memory_tip: The three circumradius vectors add to OH. Reason: the point P with OP = OA + OB + OC lies on two altitudes.
lines: For any triangle, the circumcentre O and
OP = OA + OB + OC has AP = OB + OC = 2 OD,
D the midpoint of BC, and OD ⊥ BC because
|OB| = |OC|. The same step at B gives
BP ⊥ CA, so P is on two altitudes, P = H.)

recall.must_convey: That OA + OB + OC = OH is the standard circumcentre and orthocentre result, and why it holds — the point P with that position vector lies on two altitudes.
accept: use the result that OA plus OB plus OC equals OH
the sum of the three circumradius vectors is the vector to the orthocentre
the point with that position vector lies on two altitudes so it is H
OA plus OB plus OC equals OH ane result vaadali
quote the circumcentre to orthocentre result and give its reason

steps.why: This one substitution is what converts a general statement about three position vectors into a statement about H alone. Without it the working stops at an expression, not a proof.
common_mistakes: Quoting the result with the wrong point, for example OA + OB + OC = 3 OG for the centroid, and then not converting it.
Using the result without any reason, when the question is itself about proving relations between these centres.

steps.label: Simplify to 2HO
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The working gives −2 OH, but the question asked for 2 HO. Reversing a vector changes its sign, so −OH = HO — write that line, because the two forms look different on the page.
steps.memory_tip: Reversing a vector changes its sign: −OH = HO. So −2 OH is the same as 2 HO.
lines: HA + HB + HC = OH − 3 OH = −2 OH

recall.must_convey: That OH − 3 OH = −2 OH, and that −OH = HO, so the sum equals 2 HO.
accept: OH minus three OH is minus two OH which is two HO
reversing the vector changes the sign so minus OH is HO
the answer is two HO
minus OH ante HO, so minus two OH equals two HO
substitute the result and simplify to two HO

steps.why: OH and HO are the same segment travelled in opposite directions, so they differ only in sign. Leaving the answer as −2 OH is correct mathematics but is not the form the question asked for.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as −2 OH and never turning it into 2 HO.
Writing −OH = OH and losing the sign completely.
